chapter.title: The dry timber: why Germany wanted to fight again

cards.body:
Picture a street where one house, Germany, lost a fight in 1918 and was told to pay for the whole brawl. The 1919 peace deal did not clear the yard. **It stacked dry timber against the walls**: lost land, a tiny army, a bill it could not pay, and a grudge every family in the house could feel.

Ten years later a hard winter hit the whole street, and the timber was still there, drier than ever.
cards.simpler:
Think of a street of houses. One house, Germany, lost a fight in 1918 and was told to pay for the whole brawl. The 1919 peace deal did not clean up the yard. **It piled dry timber against the walls**: lost land, a tiny army, a bill it could not pay, and a grudge the whole family felt.

Ten years later a hard winter hit the street. The timber was still there, drier than ever.

cards.prompt: Hamburg, 1930. Klaus, a dockworker, has lost his job and his savings. A man on a crate at the corner shouts that the 1919 treaty is to blame for everything and promises to tear it up. Why does Klaus stop to listen?

options.text: He has read the treaty and wants to check the speaker's facts.
He is broke and angry, and the speaker gives both feelings one target.
He hopes Germany will join the new international peace club.

whyNot.a: That's what a historian does, not a hungry man on a street corner: Klaus has no job, and the speaker is offering a feeling, not a footnote.
whyNot.c: That's the opposite mood: the peace club was part of the 1919 world the speaker is blaming, so that is not what pulls Klaus in.

cards.reteach: The timber was two things stacked together. 1919 gave Germans a grievance: lost land, a shrunken army, a bill. 1929 gave them desperation: no work, no savings. The speaker's trick is to point at the grievance as the cause of the desperation, true or not.

cards.title: 1919: the bill
cards.body:
Germany signed the *Treaty of Versailles*, the peace deal ending the First World War, on 28 June 1919. It was not allowed to negotiate. It lost about 13 percent of its land, including a strip handed to Poland that cut Germany in two.

Its army was capped at 100,000 men. It had to accept blame for the war and pay *reparations*, money for the damage, set in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks.

**Most Germans did not feel defeated. They felt cheated.** Their army had still been standing on French soil when the fighting stopped. The treaty became a wound any politician could press.
cards.simpler:
In June 1919 Germany signed the Treaty of Versailles, the war's peace deal. It was given no say. It lost about 13 percent of its land, including a strip handed to Poland that cut Germany in two.

Its army was capped at 100,000 men. It had to accept blame and pay reparations, money for damage, set in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks.

**Most Germans felt cheated, not beaten.** Their army was still in France when the fighting stopped.

cards.title: The vote that followed the breadline
cards.body:
In the May 1928 election the Nazi party won 2.6 percent of the vote. Nobody serious was worried.

In October 1929 the American stock market crashed, and the American loans Germany had been living on dried up. By September 1930 the Nazis had 18.3 percent. By July 1932, with about 6 million Germans out of work, they had 37.3 percent.

**The message had barely changed. The audience had.**
cards.simpler:
In May 1928 the Nazi party won 2.6 percent of the vote. Nobody important was worried.

In October 1929 share prices in America collapsed. The American loans Germany had been living on dried up. By September 1930 the Nazis had 18.3 percent. By July 1932, with about 6 million Germans out of work, they had 37.3 percent.

**The message had barely changed. The audience had.** The same speech lands differently in a room full of hungry people.

cards.prompt: Your friend Priya says: 'Germany went Nazi because Germans were just angrier than everyone else.' Which reply uses what you have just read?

options.text: 'Germans were angry from 1919 on, but the Nazis got 2.6 percent in 1928. The anger only turned into votes once the 1929 crash took people's jobs.'
'Right. The treaty made everyone furious, so the Nazis won big straight away in 1919.'
'The treaty did not matter. It was all about the stock market.'

whyNot.b: That's the grievance alone, not grievance plus desperation: the Nazis were a fringe party for 9 years after the treaty. Anger without hunger did not win elections.
whyNot.c: That's the desperation alone, not the pair: the crash hit Britain and America too, and they did not elect anyone like Hitler. It was the crash landing on an old grievance.

cards.reteach: Think of two ingredients. The grievance from 1919 sat there for a decade and produced a 2.6 percent party. The desperation from 1929 arrived on top of it, and within 3 years that party was the biggest in Germany. Either one alone does not get you there.

cards.title: What Hitler said he wanted
cards.body:
Hitler became *chancellor*, head of the government, on 30 January 1933. He had written his aims down in his book *Mein Kampf* years earlier, and he did not hide them. First, undo 1919: rebuild the army, take back lost land, bring all German speakers into one state.

Second, and bigger, *Lebensraum*, meaning living space: farmland in the east, in Poland and Russia, cleared of the people living there. **Undoing 1919 was the slogan. Land in the east was the plan.**

Germany was not the only house full of timber. Japan, short of oil and iron, had been at war in China since July 1937 for an empire of its own. Italy under Mussolini had invaded Ethiopia in 1935 and wanted more.
cards.simpler:
Hitler became chancellor, head of government, on 30 January 1933. His book Mein Kampf had set out his aims years before. First, undo 1919: rebuild the army, win back land, unite German speakers. Second, bigger: Lebensraum, living space, meaning farmland in Poland and Russia cleared of its people.

**Undoing 1919 was the slogan. Land in the east was the plan.**

Japan, short of oil and iron, had fought in China since 1937. Italy had invaded Ethiopia in 1935. Both wanted empires.

cards.body:
Tom finishes a documentary and tells his flatmate the treaty 'caused' Hitler, as if 1919 made 1939 unavoidable. But for 9 years after Versailles the Nazis stayed on the fringe, and in 1928 they got 2.6 percent.

**Spot the mistake when someone jumps from 1919 straight to 1933** with nothing in between. The missing piece is 1929, when the money ran out.
cards.simpler:
Tom watches a documentary and tells his flatmate the treaty 'caused' Hitler, as if 1919 made 1939 certain. But for 9 years after Versailles the Nazis stayed small and ignored. In 1928 they won just 2.6 percent.

**Watch for the jump from 1919 straight to 1933** with nothing in between. The missing step is 1929, the year the money ran out. A dry pile of timber still needs a match.

cards.prompt: A pub quiz asks: what turned Germany from a sore loser in 1919 into a country ready to fight in 1939? Pick the fullest answer.

options.text: The 1919 treaty alone. Humiliation always leads to war.
A grievance from 1919, desperation from the 1929 crash, and from 1933 a leader who promised to turn both into revenge and land.
Hitler alone. Without him Germans would have been content.

whyNot.a: That's the timber without the match: humiliated countries do not always fight. For 9 years after 1919 the Nazis stayed on the fringe.
whyNot.c: That's the match without the timber: Hitler had the same message in 1928 and got 2.6 percent. He needed the crash to be heard.

cards.reteach: Three dates, three layers. 1919 left a wound. 1929 left millions without work and made the wound feel like the cause. 1933 put in charge a man who had promised, in writing, to tear up the treaty and take land in the east.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
**Germany in 1939 was a house of dry timber**: 1919 left it humiliated and in debt, 1929 left it broke and jobless, and from 1933 Hitler promised to turn both into revenge on the treaty and farmland in the east.

Japan and Italy had their own grudges and wanted empires too, so three houses on the street were ready to burn.
cards.simpler:
**Germany in 1939 was a house of dry timber.** The 1919 treaty left it shamed and in debt. The 1929 crash left it broke and out of work. From 1933 Hitler promised to turn both into revenge on the treaty and farmland in the east.

Japan and Italy carried their own grudges and wanted empires too. So three houses on the street were ready to burn.

cards.body: Tonight, tell someone the story in three sentences: what 1919 did, what 1929 did, what Hitler promised. If it takes you more than 30 seconds, you are adding too much.
cards.simpler: Tonight, tell someone the story in three sentences. One for what 1919 did. One for what 1929 did. One for what Hitler promised. Time yourself. If it takes more than 30 seconds, you are adding too much. **Three sentences, 30 seconds, nothing extra.** Think of it like giving directions: the shortest route is the one people remember.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain in three plain sentences why Germany in 1939 was willing to fight a war it had lost so badly 21 years earlier.
